A question that sometimes arises is what should happen if a CPU tries to acquire a lock that the same CPU already holds. One line of reasoning is that this should be allowed: no other CPU can hold the lock, so there’s no need to worry about CPUs interfering with each others’ use of the protected data. Locking systems that allow a CPU to re-acquire a lock it already holds are called a re-entrant or recursive. On the other hand, if a lock is already held, even on the same CPU, that means an operation may have temporarily violated and not yet restored some invariants; to allow a new operation to commence while the invariants don’t hold seems like an invitation to bugs. Xv6 takes this latter view, and forbids a CPU that currently holds a lock from re-acquiring it. Detecting this situation is the purpose of the call to holding in acquire.

7.5 Locks and interrupts

Some xv6 spinlocks protect data that is used by both threads and interrupt handlers. For example, the clockintr timer interrupt handler might increment ticks at about the same time that a kernel thread reads ticks in sys_pause. The lock tickslock serializes the two accesses.

The interaction of spinlocks and interrupts raises a potential danger. Suppose sys_pause holds tickslock, and its CPU is interrupted by a timer interrupt. clockintr would try to acquire tickslock, see it was held, and wait for it to be released. In this situation, tickslock will never be released: only sys_pause can release it, but sys_pause will not continue running until clockintr returns. So the CPU will deadlock, and any code that needs either lock will also freeze.

To avoid this situation, if a spinlock is used by an interrupt handler, a CPU must never hold that lock with interrupts enabled. Xv6 is more conservative: when a CPU acquires any lock, xv6 always disables interrupts on that CPU. Interrupts may still occur on other CPUs, so an interrupt’s acquire can wait for a thread to release a spinlock; just not on the same CPU.

Most kernels, including xv6, interleave the execution of multiple activities. One source of interleaving is multiprocessor hardware: computers with multiple CPUs executing independently, such as xv6’s RISC-V. These multiple CPUs share physical RAM, and xv6 exploits the sharing to maintain kernel data structures that all CPUs read and write. This sharing raises the possibility of one CPU reading a data structure while another CPU is mid-way through updating it, or even multiple CPUs updating the same data simultaneously; without careful design such parallel access is likely to yield incorrect results or a broken data structure. Even on a uniprocessor, the kernel may switch the CPU among a number of threads, causing their execution to be interleaved. Finally, a device interrupt handler that modifies the same data as some interruptible code could damage the data if the interrupt occurs just as the interrupted code is also modifying the data. The word concurrency refers to situations in which multiple instruction streams are interleaved, due to multiprocessor parallelism, thread switching, or interrupts.

Xv6 has two types of locks: spinlocks and sleep-locks. We’ll start with spinlocks. Xv6 represents a spinlock as a struct spinlock. Unfortunately, this implementation does not guarantee mutual exclusion in the face of concurrency. Two CPUs could simultaneously reach line 25, see that lk->locked is zero, and then both grab the lock by executing line 26. At this point, two different CPUs hold the lock, which violates the mutual exclusion property. What we need is a way to make lines 25 and 26 execute as an atomic (indivisible) step.

response.title: Spinlock and Interrupt Synchronization Design
response.evidence_note: The evidence covers xv6 spinlocks, the danger of interrupt handlers acquiring locks held by interrupted code, and xv6's conservative strategy of disabling interrupts on a CPU when any lock is acquired. It also covers multiprocessor interleaving and the distinction that interrupts may still occur on other CPUs. This is sufficient for a hard short-answer design evaluation.

questions.stem:
A kernel thread and a timer interrupt handler share a spinlock `tickslock`. The thread acquires `tickslock` in `sys_pause` and then calls a helper function that may block waiting for disk I/O. The interrupt handler `clockintr` also tries to acquire `tickslock`. The system may run on a multiprocessor.

Evaluate this design. In your answer:
1. Explain the deadlock that can occur if the thread holds `tickslock` with interrupts enabled on the same CPU.
2. State what xv6 does when any lock is acquired, and explain why that rule prevents the deadlock on the same CPU.
3. Explain whether the same deadlock can occur on another CPU that is running the interrupt handler concurrently.
4. Given that the thread may block while holding `tickslock`, identify an additional problem and propose a lock type or design change that avoids it.

Provide a concise justification for each point.
questions.answer:
1. If `sys_pause` holds `tickslock` and is interrupted by `clockintr` on the same CPU, `clockintr` tries to acquire `tickslock`, sees it is held, and spins waiting for release. Only `sys_pause` can release it, but `sys_pause` cannot continue until `clockintr` returns. This is a deadlock.

2. In xv6, when a CPU acquires any spinlock, xv6 disables interrupts on that CPU. This prevents the timer interrupt from firing on the same CPU while the lock is held, so `clockintr` cannot try to acquire `tickslock` on that CPU and the same-CPU deadlock is avoided.

3. On another CPU, the interrupt handler may still run and try to acquire `tickslock`. It may spin waiting for the thread to release the lock, but it does not deadlock the original CPU because the original thread can continue and eventually release the lock. xv6 allows an interrupt's acquire to wait for a thread to release a spinlock, just not on the same CPU.

4. If the thread blocks while holding `tickslock` (for example, waiting for disk I/O), it may delay release of the spinlock for a long time, causing other CPUs or interrupt handlers to spin-wait and waste CPU or stall. Spinlocks are not designed to be held across blocking operations. A better design is to release `tickslock` before blocking or to protect the shared data with a sleep-lock that allows the holder to sleep while waiting.
questions.explanation: The scenario combines interrupt handling, spinlock semantics, and multiprocessor effects. The key same-CPU danger is that an interrupt handler acquires the lock held by the interrupted thread, so the thread can never release it. xv6 avoids this by disabling interrupts on a CPU when any lock is acquired. On other CPUs, waiting is possible but does not freeze the original CPU. Finally, blocking while holding a spinlock is unsafe because spinlocks are meant for short critical sections without sleeping; a sleep-lock or releasing the lock before blocking is appropriate.
questions.difficulty_reason: The question requires integrating spinlock semantics, interrupt handling, multiprocessor concurrency, and the distinction between spinlocks and sleep-locks. It asks the student to evaluate a concrete design with multiple interacting constraints, identify a deadlock and a blocking hazard, and justify a design change, which is analysis and evaluation rather than recall or simple application.

expected_steps: Explain the same-CPU deadlock: interrupt handler spins for a lock held by the interrupted thread, which cannot run to release it.
State that xv6 disables interrupts on a CPU when acquiring any lock and explain that this prevents the same-CPU interrupt from acquiring the held lock.
Explain that on another CPU the interrupt handler may wait for the lock, but this does not deadlock the original CPU; the thread can still release.
Identify that blocking while holding a spinlock is unsafe and propose releasing the lock before blocking or using a sleep-lock.

1. Deadlock on the same CPU: Suppose sys_pause holds tickslock with interrupts enabled on a CPU. A timer interrupt arrives; the CPU starts running clockintr, which tries to acquire tickslock. Because the lock is already held by the interrupted sys_pause on the same CPU, clockintr spins forever waiting for release. But sys_pause cannot release the lock because it is not running: the interrupt handler has taken over the CPU and will not return until clockintr finishes. Thus the CPU deadlocks, and any code needing tickslock also freezes.

2. What xv6 does: When a CPU acquires any lock, xv6 disables interrupts on that CPU. Since the CPU cannot be interrupted while it holds tickslock, clockintr cannot run on the same CPU and therefore cannot spin waiting for a lock held by the interrupted thread. This prevents the same-CPU deadlock. Interrupts may still occur on other CPUs.

3. Another CPU: On a different CPU, clockintr can run concurrently and may try to acquire tickslock while the first CPU's thread holds it. This does not cause the same interrupted-thread deadlock because the holder is on a different CPU and can continue running and eventually release the lock. The other CPU may spin briefly until the lock is released, which is normal spinlock behavior, not deadlock.

4. Blocking while holding a spinlock: Spinlocks are not designed to be held while blocking (e.g. waiting for disk I/O). If the thread blocks while holding tickslock, interrupts on that CPU may remain disabled (since xv6 disables interrupts on lock acquisition) and the CPU cannot make progress on other work; moreover, other CPUs and interrupt handlers spin waiting for tickslock, wasting CPU and potentially delaying the release until I/O completes. To avoid this, use a sleep-lock (mutex) rather than a spinlock for data shared with interrupt handlers, or restructure the code so the thread does not block while holding tickslock. Care is needed because sleep-locks cannot be acquired in interrupt context; an alternative is to release the spinlock, perform the blocking I/O, then reacquire, or use a separate lock hierarchy. The key is not to hold a spinlock across a blocking operation.

questions.stem:
A kernel thread and a timer interrupt handler share a spinlock `tickslock`. The thread acquires `tickslock` in `sys_pause` and then calls a helper function that may block waiting for disk I/O. The interrupt handler `clockintr` also tries to acquire `tickslock`. The system may run on a multiprocessor.

Evaluate this design. In your answer:
1. Explain the deadlock that can occur if the thread holds `tickslock` with interrupts enabled on the same CPU.
2. State what xv6 does when any lock is acquired, and explain why that rule prevents the deadlock on the same CPU.
3. Explain whether the same deadlock can occur on another CPU that is running the interrupt handler concurrently.
4. Given that the thread may block while holding `tickslock`, identify an additional problem and propose a lock type or design change that avoids it.

Provide a concise justification for each point.
questions.answer:
1. If `sys_pause` holds `tickslock` and is interrupted by `clockintr` on the same CPU, `clockintr` tries to acquire `tickslock`, sees it is held, and spins waiting for release. Only `sys_pause` can release it, but `sys_pause` cannot continue until `clockintr` returns. This is a deadlock.

2. In xv6, when a CPU acquires any spinlock, xv6 disables interrupts on that CPU. This prevents the timer interrupt from firing on the same CPU while the lock is held, so `clockintr` cannot try to acquire `tickslock` on that CPU and the same-CPU deadlock is avoided.

3. On another CPU, the interrupt handler may still run and try to acquire `tickslock`. It may spin waiting for the thread to release the lock, but it does not deadlock the original CPU because the original thread can continue and eventually release the lock. xv6 allows an interrupt's acquire to wait for a thread to release a spinlock, just not on the same CPU.

4. If the thread blocks while holding `tickslock` (for example, waiting for disk I/O), it may delay release of the spinlock for a long time, causing other CPUs or interrupt handlers to spin-wait and waste CPU or stall. Spinlocks are not designed to be held across blocking operations. A better design is to release `tickslock` before blocking or to protect the shared data with a sleep-lock that allows the holder to sleep while waiting.
questions.explanation: The scenario combines interrupt handling, spinlock semantics, and multiprocessor effects. The key same-CPU danger is that an interrupt handler acquires the lock held by the interrupted thread, so the thread can never release it. xv6 avoids this by disabling interrupts on a CPU when any lock is acquired. On other CPUs, waiting is possible but does not freeze the original CPU. Finally, blocking while holding a spinlock is unsafe because spinlocks are meant for short critical sections without sleeping; a sleep-lock or releasing the lock before blocking is appropriate.

Consider xv6 running on a multiprocessor RISC-V system. A kernel thread function sys_pause executes `acquire(&tickslock); ticks = ticks + 1; release(&tickslock);` and a timer interrupt handler clockintr does the same on some CPU. The spinlock tickslock protects the shared variable ticks and is used by both the kernel thread and the interrupt handler.

Suppose sys_pause has just executed acquire(&tickslock) and is about to execute the increment, but the CPU it is running on is interrupted by a timer interrupt before it reaches release(&tickslock).

Answer the following:

1. According to xv6's lock implementation, what would clockintr do when it tries to acquire tickslock in this situation, and why?
2. What must xv6 do when acquiring any spinlock to prevent this specific deadlock, and what is the exact condition for this rule to apply? Explain why this rule prevents the deadlock on the same CPU but still allows interrupt handlers on other CPUs to contend for the lock.
3. If two different CPUs are both executing code that tries to acquire tickslock at the same time, and neither CPU currently holds it, what mechanism in xv6 ensures that only one CPU succeeds in acquiring the lock? Explain why a simple check of lk->locked followed by setting it is insufficient.
4. Could the same deadlock occur if the interrupt handler runs on a CPU that is not currently holding tickslock, while another CPU holds it? Justify your answer.

Provide a concise but complete justification for each part. Your answer should reference the relevant xv6 mechanisms and reasoning from the supplied material.
questions.answer:
1. clockintr would try to acquire tickslock, see that it is held, and spin (wait) for it to be released. It will spin indefinitely on the same CPU because only sys_pause can release tickslock, but sys_pause cannot continue running until clockintr returns. This causes a deadlock on that CPU [context_18ed3aab01b029acd8c1aa100b6ea664].

2. When a CPU acquires any spinlock, xv6 disables interrupts on that CPU. The rule applies whenever a spinlock is used by an interrupt handler (and xv6 is conservative: it does this for every lock acquisition). If sys_pause acquires tickslock with interrupts disabled, the timer interrupt cannot occur on that CPU, so clockintr cannot run on that CPU and cannot try to acquire tickslock while sys_pause holds it, preventing the self-deadlock. Interrupts can still occur on other CPUs, so clockintr on a different CPU can contend for tickslock; it may spin waiting for sys_pause to release, but that other CPU is not the one holding the lock, so sys_pause can continue and eventually release the lock [context_18ed3aab01b029acd8c1aa100b6ea664].

3. xv6 spinlocks guarantee mutual exclusion through an atomic test-and-set (or equivalent atomic instruction) that checks and sets lk->locked in one indivisible step. A simple read of lk->locked followed by a write is not sufficient because two CPUs could simultaneously read zero and both proceed to set the lock, resulting in both holding the lock. The atomic operation ensures only one CPU observes the lock as free and successfully acquires it, while the other must spin [context_721949419795d5384fb58f88476a0eb7].

4. No. If the interrupt handler runs on a CPU that does not hold tickslock, and another CPU holds it, the handler will spin waiting for the lock to be released. The CPU holding the lock can continue executing (it is not interrupted by that handler on its own CPU) and will eventually release tickslock, allowing the waiting handler to proceed. The deadlock in part 1 specifically required the interrupt to preempt the same CPU that holds the lock; cross-CPU waiting does not prevent the lock holder from making progress [context_18ed3aab01b029acd8c1aa100b6ea664].
questions.explanation:
Part 1: The danger is a self-deadlock: the interrupted code holds the lock and cannot run to release it, while the interrupt handler on the same CPU spins forever waiting for that lock [context_18ed3aab01b029acd8c1aa100b6ea664].
Part 2: xv6 disables interrupts on a CPU when it acquires any spinlock. This prevents the same CPU from being interrupted and re-entering a lock it already holds. Other CPUs are unaffected, so they can still contend for the lock; the holder can still release it because the holder is not the one spinning [context_18ed3aab01b029acd8c1aa100b6ea664].
Part 3: Mutual exclusion for spinlocks requires an atomic operation (such as atomic exchange or test-and-set) on lk->locked. Without atomicity, two CPUs could both read the lock as free and both believe they acquired it [context_721949419795d5384fb58f88476a0eb7].
Part 4: Cross-CPU waiting is safe because the lock holder continues executing and can release the lock. The deadlock only arises when the waiting handler runs on the same CPU that holds the lock, preventing that CPU from releasing it [context_18ed3aab01b029acd8c1aa100b6ea664].

These must be combined to justify why the rule prevents same-CPU deadlock while still allowing cross-CPU contention. Explain that other CPUs can still contend for the lock because they are not the holder and can spin while the holder releases it.

response.answer:
1. On the same CPU, clockintr would attempt to acquire tickslock, find that the CPU already holds it, and must not spin waiting for release. In xv6, a CPU that already holds a lock cannot re-acquire it; acquire detects this via holding(). Here, spinning would deadlock because the interrupted thread sys_pause cannot release tickslock until clockintr returns, but clockintr cannot proceed until the lock is released. Thus the situation is the forbidden self-deadlock/re-acquisition case.

2. When acquiring any spinlock, xv6 disables interrupts on the CPU acquiring the lock. The relevant condition for the stronger always-disable approach is: xv6 chooses to do this for every lock, not only locks known to be used by interrupt handlers. Conceptually, the needed rule would be to disable interrupts on a CPU whenever it holds a spinlock that an interrupt handler on that same CPU might try to acquire. Disabling interrupts prevents the same CPU from taking a timer interrupt while holding the lock, so its interrupt handler cannot run and try to acquire the same lock. Other CPUs still have interrupts enabled, so their interrupt handlers may attempt to acquire tickslock; they can spin until the holder releases it, because the holder on the first CPU can still run and release the lock.

3. On two different CPUs, if neither holds tickslock, only one can succeed because acquisition uses an atomic read-modify-write instruction, typically an atomic swap/test-and-set implemented in RISC-V as amoswap or similar atomic exchange. That instruction atomically reads the old value and writes a nonzero/locked value. A simple load of lk->locked followed by a store is insufficient because two CPUs can both load zero before either stores; both then store and both believe they acquired the lock, violating mutual exclusion. The atomic exchange ensures exactly one CPU observes the old value as zero.

4. No, the same deadlock does not occur if the interrupt handler runs on a CPU that is not holding tickslock while another CPU holds it. In that case the interrupt handler may spin waiting for tickslock, but the holder is on a different CPU and is not prevented from running by this interrupt; it can eventually release the lock. The deadlock in part 1 is specific to the interrupting CPU itself already holding the lock, so the handler and interrupted code are on the same CPU.

Consider xv6 running on a multiprocessor RISC-V system. A kernel thread function sys_pause executes `acquire(&tickslock); ticks = ticks + 1; release(&tickslock);` and a timer interrupt handler clockintr does the same on some CPU. The spinlock tickslock protects the shared variable ticks and is used by both the kernel thread and the interrupt handler.

1. According to xv6's lock implementation, what would clockintr do when it tries to acquire tickslock in this situation, and why?
2. What must xv6 do when acquiring any spinlock to prevent this specific deadlock, and what is the exact condition for this rule to apply? Explain why this rule prevents the deadlock on the same CPU but still allows interrupt handlers on other CPUs to contend for the lock.
3. If two different CPUs are both executing code that tries to acquire tickslock at the same time, and neither CPU currently holds it, what mechanism in xv6 ensures that only one CPU succeeds in acquiring the lock? Explain why a simple check of lk->locked followed by setting it is insufficient.
4. Could the same deadlock occur if the interrupt handler runs on a CPU that is not currently holding tickslock, while another CPU holds it? Justify your answer.

Provide a concise but complete justification for each part. Your answer should reference the relevant xv6 mechanisms and reasoning from the supplied material.

1. clockintr would try to acquire tickslock, see that it is held, and spin (wait) for it to be released. It will spin indefinitely on the same CPU because only sys_pause can release tickslock, but sys_pause cannot continue running until clockintr returns. This causes a deadlock on that CPU [context_18ed3aab01b029acd8c1aa100b6ea664].

2. When a CPU acquires any spinlock, xv6 disables interrupts on that CPU. The rule applies whenever a spinlock is used by an interrupt handler (and xv6 is conservative: it does this for every lock acquisition). If sys_pause acquires tickslock with interrupts disabled, the timer interrupt cannot occur on that CPU, so clockintr cannot run on that CPU and cannot try to acquire tickslock while sys_pause holds it, preventing the self-deadlock. Interrupts can still occur on other CPUs, so clockintr on a different CPU can contend for tickslock; it may spin waiting for sys_pause to release, but that other CPU is not the one holding the lock, so sys_pause can continue and eventually release the lock [context_18ed3aab01b029acd8c1aa100b6ea664].

3. xv6 spinlocks guarantee mutual exclusion through an atomic test-and-set (or equivalent atomic instruction) that checks and sets lk->locked in one indivisible step. A simple read of lk->locked followed by a write is not sufficient because two CPUs could simultaneously read zero and both proceed to set the lock, resulting in both holding the lock. The atomic operation ensures only one CPU observes the lock as free and successfully acquires it, while the other must spin [context_721949419795d5384fb58f88476a0eb7].

4. No. If the interrupt handler runs on a CPU that does not hold tickslock, and another CPU holds it, the handler will spin waiting for the lock to be released. The CPU holding the lock can continue executing (it is not interrupted by that handler on its own CPU) and will eventually release tickslock, allowing the waiting handler to proceed. The deadlock in part 1 specifically required the interrupt to preempt the same CPU that holds the lock; cross-CPU waiting does not prevent the lock holder from making progress [context_18ed3aab01b029acd8c1aa100b6ea664].

response.title: Spinlock and Interrupt Handler Synchronization Design
response.evidence_note: The supplied sources cover re-entrant lock policy in xv6, the lock/interrupt deadlock scenario (tickslock example with sys_pause and clockintr), the conservative acquire-always-disables-interrupts policy, cross-CPU interrupt behavior, and spinlock mutual exclusion semantics. These are sufficient for a hard short-answer design-evaluation question without invoking a scheduler tool.

questions.stem:
A kernel is being modified so that a kernel thread in sys_pause and a timer interrupt handler clockintr both access ticks. The lock tickslock serializes the two accesses.

Some designers propose the following change: the thread should disable interrupts only on code paths that it knows can be interrupted by clockintr, and leave interrupts enabled while holding tickslock on other paths. They also propose that if the thread already holds tickslock and is interrupted by clockintr, then when clockintr tries to acquire tickslock, the acquire routine should hand the lock to clockintr because the interrupted thread already owns the lock.

1. The thread's interrupt-disabling code is removed; the thread holds tickslock with interrupts enabled.
2. clockintr runs on the same CPU while the thread holds tickslock.
3. clockintr calls acquire on tickslock.
4. If the acquire sees the lock is held, the proposed routine lets clockintr proceed with the lock.

Using the supplied xv6 semantics, evaluate whether this proposal is safe. In your answer, identify the deadlock that arises from the original ordering, explain what property of the proposed hand-off violates xv6's lock rules, and state what xv6 does to prevent the same-CPU deadlock when a spinlock is used by an interrupt handler. Then explain why interrupts on other CPUs still require the spinlock.
questions.answer:
The proposal is not safe.

Original deadlock ordering: if sys_pause holds tickslock with interrupts enabled and the same CPU is then interrupted by the timer interrupt, clockintr tries to acquire tickslock, sees it held, and waits. tickslock will never be released because only sys_pause can release it, and sys_pause cannot continue until clockintr returns. So the CPU deadlocks, and any code needing either lock also freezes.

Hand-off violation: xv6 forbids a CPU that currently holds a lock from re-acquiring it; detecting this is the purpose of the holding call in acquire. Letting clockintr proceed while the interrupted thread still holds tickslock means the same CPU holds the lock twice, violating xv6's non-re-entrant rule. It also lets a new operation run while invariants protected by tickslock may be temporarily violated and not yet restored.

What xv6 does: when a CPU acquires any lock, xv6 always disables interrupts on that CPU. This prevents a same-CPU interrupt handler from attempting to acquire a lock the CPU already holds. Interrupts may still occur on other CPUs, so an interrupt's acquire can wait for a thread to release a spinlock; just not on the same CPU. Because the other CPUs can still enter the interrupt handler and contend for tickslock, the spinlock is still required to serialize the thread's and handler's accesses across CPUs.
questions.explanation: Correct reasoning must use the supplied xv6 facts: a same-CPU acquire of an already-held lock deadlocks because the holder cannot run until the handler returns, xv6 forbids re-acquisition by the same CPU through the holding check, and xv6 disables interrupts on the acquiring CPU whenever any lock is acquired. The hand-off proposal is exactly the re-acquisition xv6 forbids, so it does not restore safety. Cross-CPU interrupts are still possible, so disabling local interrupts does not remove the need for spinlock serialization of the shared data.
questions.difficulty_reason: The learner must integrate three supplied mechanisms: the same-CPU interrupt/lock deadlock, xv6's non-re-entrant lock rule with its holding check, and the acquire-disables-interrupts policy. The question requires judging a concrete proposed design (a same-CPU hand-off and selective interrupt disabling) against those interacting constraints and explaining why the multiprocessor case still needs the spinlock, rather than recalling a single definition.

xv6 non-re-entrant lock policy and holding check
disabling interrupts on the acquiring CPU when any lock is acquired

expected_steps: Explain the original same-CPU deadlock: the thread holds tickslock, the interrupt handler waits on tickslock, and the thread cannot release it until the handler returns.
Identify the proposed hand-off as a violation of xv6's rule against a CPU re-acquiring a lock it already holds, detectable via holding in acquire.
State that xv6 disables interrupts on a CPU whenever it acquires any lock, preventing same-CPU handler re-acquisition.
Justify that the spinlock is still needed because interrupts on other CPUs can contend for tickslock.

response.answer: The proposal is not safe. Original same-CPU deadlock: if sys_pause holds tickslock with interrupts enabled and clockintr interrupts that same CPU, clockintr tries to acquire tickslock, finds it held, and spins waiting for sys_pause to release it. But sys_pause cannot run to release tickslock until clockintr returns, and clockintr cannot return until it acquires tickslock. So the CPU spins forever; no progress is possible. The proposed hand-off violates xv6's lock rules because xv6 spinlocks are not re-entrant/recursive: a CPU that already holds a lock may not acquire it again, and acquire detects this with holding. Letting clockintr 'proceed with the lock' would allow two executions on the same CPU to hold the same lock at once, violating mutual exclusion and using the protected data (ticks) while invariants may be temporarily broken. xv6 prevents the same-CPU deadlock by disabling interrupts on a CPU whenever that CPU acquires any spinlock; more generally, if a spinlock may be used by an interrupt handler, that CPU must never hold the lock with interrupts enabled. Other CPUs still require the spinlock because xv6 runs on a multiprocessor: interrupts can occur on other CPUs, and those CPUs can attempt to acquire tickslock concurrently with a thread on a different CPU. Interrupt disabling on one CPU does not stop other CPUs from running clockintr or accessing ticks, so tickslock is still needed for mutual exclusion across CPUs. The other-CPU acquire may wait for the lock release, but it is not a same-CPU self-deadlock.

questions.answer:
The proposal is not safe.

Original deadlock ordering: if sys_pause holds tickslock with interrupts enabled and the same CPU is then interrupted by the timer interrupt, clockintr tries to acquire tickslock, sees it held, and waits. tickslock will never be released because only sys_pause can release it, and sys_pause cannot continue until clockintr returns. So the CPU deadlocks, and any code needing either lock also freezes.

Hand-off violation: xv6 forbids a CPU that currently holds a lock from re-acquiring it; detecting this is the purpose of the holding call in acquire. Letting clockintr proceed while the interrupted thread still holds tickslock means the same CPU holds the lock twice, violating xv6's non-re-entrant rule. It also lets a new operation run while invariants protected by tickslock may be temporarily violated and not yet restored.

What xv6 does: when a CPU acquires any lock, xv6 always disables interrupts on that CPU. This prevents a same-CPU interrupt handler from attempting to acquire a lock the CPU already holds. Interrupts may still occur on other CPUs, so an interrupt's acquire can wait for a thread to release a spinlock; just not on the same CPU. Because the other CPUs can still enter the interrupt handler and contend for tickslock, the spinlock is still required to serialize the thread's and handler's accesses across CPUs.

A question that sometimes arises is what should happen if a CPU tries to acquire a lock that the same CPU already holds. One line of reasoning is that this should be allowed: no other CPU can hold the lock, so there’s no need to worry about CPUs interfering with each others’ use of the protected data. Locking systems that allow a CPU to re-acquire a lock it already holds are called a re-entrant or recursive. On the other hand, if a lock is already held, even on the same CPU, that means an operation may have temporarily violated and not yet restored some invariants; to allow a new operation to commence while the invariants don’t hold seems like an invitation to bugs. Xv6 takes this latter view, and forbids a CPU that currently holds a lock from re-acquiring it. Detecting this situation is the purpose of the call to holding in acquire.

7.5 Locks and interrupts

Some xv6 spinlocks protect data that is used by both threads and interrupt handlers. For example, the clockintr timer interrupt handler might increment ticks at about the same time that a kernel thread reads ticks in sys_pause. The lock tickslock serializes the two accesses.

The interaction of spinlocks and interrupts raises a potential danger. Suppose sys_pause holds tickslock, and its CPU is interrupted by a timer interrupt. clockintr would try to acquire tickslock, see it was held, and wait for it to be released. In this situation, tickslock will never be released: only sys_pause can release it, but sys_pause will not continue running until clockintr returns. So the CPU will deadlock, and any code that needs either lock will also freeze.

To avoid this situation, if a spinlock is used by an interrupt handler, a CPU must never hold that lock with interrupts enabled. Xv6 is more conservative: when a CPU acquires any lock, xv6 always disables interrupts on that CPU. Interrupts may still occur on other CPUs, so an interrupt’s acquire can wait for a thread to release a spinlock; just not on the same CPU.

Most kernels, including xv6, interleave the execution of multiple activities. One source of interleaving is multiprocessor hardware: computers with multiple CPUs executing independently, such as xv6’s RISC-V. These multiple CPUs share physical RAM, and xv6 exploits the sharing to maintain kernel data structures that all CPUs read and write. This sharing raises the possibility of one CPU reading a data structure while another CPU is mid-way through updating it, or even multiple CPUs updating the same data simultaneously; without careful design such parallel access is likely to yield incorrect results or a broken data structure. Even on a uniprocessor, the kernel may switch the CPU among a number of threads, causing their execution to be interleaved. Finally, a device interrupt handler that modifies the same data as some interruptible code could damage the data if the interrupt occurs just as the interrupted code is also modifying the data. The word concurrency refers to situations in which multiple instruction streams are interleaved, due to multiprocessor parallelism, thread switching, or interrupts.
